title: Is the controller display on?
text: If nothing runs on any zone, start with the controller and its power before looking at individual valves. Display is dead The controller has no power Display is on The controller has power — continue

title: Check the transformer output at the controller.
text: Meter to VAC, leads on the two 24 volt input terminals where the transformer wires land. Run a zone first if the controller only supplies power while a zone is on. Between 24 and 30 VAC Transformer output is good — continue Not in range, or no reading The transformer or its connections

title: Check the common connection at the controller.
text: Look at the common (COM) terminal and the wire landed on it. Common problems at the controller are one of the most frequent reasons nothing runs. Loose, corroded, missing, or not seated Found a bad common connection at the controller Looks good Continue to the valve boxes

title: Check the common in the valve boxes.
text: The common is usually daisy-chained from valve to valve. If one leg of the chain has dropped, every valve past that point loses its common and will not run. Found a dropped or loose common leg Everything past that point is affected Common is intact in every box I can reach Continue

title: Does the system have a master valve or a pump start relay?
text: Both are wired off the controller and the common. A fault in either one can stop every zone. Yes Check the master valve or pump start circuit No, or not sure Work one zone at a time

title: Check voltage on a pulsing zone at the controller.
text: Meter to VAC, leads on COM and the zone terminal. If several valves are pulsing, check all of them. Steady, over 18 VAC Controller side looks fine — problem is at the valve Steady under 18 VAC, or fluctuating over 5 VAC Suspect the controller or its power No steady reading over 5 VAC Not an electrical problem

title: Unplug the controller, count to three, plug it back in. Check voltage again.
text: Over 18 VAC, steady or not Isolate controller from wiring Still not over 18 VAC Go test at the valve

title: At the valve box, disconnect the wires to the valve and turn the zone on. Check voltage.
text: Meter to VAC, leads on the common and the zone wire coming from the controller. Over 18 VAC Power is reaching the valve Under 18 VAC Power is being lost in the wire — split the splice from the run

title: Voltage is not coming from your controller
text: No reading at the terminal, but a reading on the zone wire, means something else is energizing that wire. Look for a second controller, a crossed wire, or induced voltage on a long parallel run.

title: Problem is the controller
text: Voltage is present on the terminal with the valve wire removed, so the controller is putting it out on its own.

title: Diode or zone doubler present
text: This guide does not cover troubleshooting past a diode or doubler. Track down the wire that actually feeds the valve you are working on and test from there.

title: Resolved
text: Verify by running the zone through a normal cycle before you leave.

title: Mechanical, not electrical
text: There is not enough voltage present for this to be an electrical fault. Check the valve and the master valve for a pressure regulator, or a bad diaphragm.

title: No wire on the terminal
text: That is the problem. Find where the zone wire went and land it.

title: Dropped common in the valve boxes
text: Remake the broken connection with a new direct-bury connector, not the one you took off. Run the zones past that point to confirm.

title: Bad common connection at the controller
text: Clean and reseat the common wire at the COM terminal, or cut back to clean copper and land it again. Run the zones to confirm.

title: Master valve or pump start circuit
text: Check the master valve and pump start relay wiring and common, and the voltage on their circuit when a zone is commanded on. If they are good, continue with the single-zone steps from the controller.

title: Controller has no power
text: Check the power source first: the outlet or breaker, then the transformer and its connections, then the controller fuse. Read the power at each point in turn until you find where it stops.

title: Transformer output is out of range
text: Check the connections where the transformer wires land at the controller, then the transformer itself and its line-side supply. If the connections are good and the output is still out of range, the transformer is the likely problem.

title: Voltage present after power cycling
text: Remove the valve wire and test at the terminal again. Still a reading at the terminal — the problem is the controller. No reading at the terminal, but a reading between common and the zone wire — the voltage is not coming from your controller.

title: Over 18 VAC at the valve
text: Reconnect a solenoid and test the voltage again. If it still reads over 18 VAC, try a new solenoid. If it still will not work and the voltage is under 21 VAC, that valve may need more voltage than the run is delivering. If voltage is good and a new solenoid does not fix it, the problem is the valve itself. Take it apart and look.

title: Problem is probably at the valve
text: Nothing is holding it open electrically. To confirm, remove the zone wire and see whether it shuts off.

title: Short in the wire run
text: With the wires apart at the valve and the solenoid out of the circuit, the zone wire and the common still read as connected. Somewhere in the run the insulation is damaged and the two conductors are touching. Ask whether anyone has dug along the wire route in the last few years: new landscaping, a fence, a trench, a sprinkler or utility repair. Digging is the most common cause of damaged wire. Finding the exact spot takes a wire tracer or fault locator, which is beyond this guide.

title: The splice was the fault
text: The wire run between the controller and the valve is intact, so the loss was in the connection, not the conductor. Cut back past the corroded copper to clean wire and remake the splice with new direct-bury connectors — not the ones you just took off, and not dry wire nuts. Reconnect the solenoid, run the zone, and recheck the voltage at the valve. It should now read over 18 VAC. If it is still low or the zone still will not run, the cable may also be damaged. Separate the splice again, keep the two wires apart, and read the zone at the controller. It should read open (OL); a low reading means the wire itself is damaged.

title: No steady voltage over 18 VAC
text: Turn on a known working zone and check its voltage. If that zone reads the same, the transformer is the likely problem. If that zone reads 18–30 VAC, the problem may be the controller. If there is a spare station, move the wire to it and see whether the zone runs.

title: Voltage present but out of range
text: Unplug the controller power, count to three, and plug it back in. Test again. If it still will not read 24–30 VAC, suspect a bad controller or transformer.

title: Over 18 VAC at the valve
text: Reconnect a solenoid and test again. If it still reads over 18 VAC, try a new solenoid. If it still will not run and the voltage is under 21 VAC, that valve may need more voltage than the run is delivering. Troubleshoot the wire path.

title: Problem is in the wiring
text: Voltage is leaving the controller but not arriving at the valve. Ask whether anyone has dug along the wire route in the last few years: new landscaping, a fence, a trench, a sprinkler or utility repair. Digging is the most common cause of damaged wire. Pinpointing the damage takes a wire tracer or fault locator.

title: Is the zone showing as on at the controller?
text: Yes — turn the dial to off and wait 30 seconds Then check whether the zone shuts off No, controller shows it off Check the electrical side anyway

title: Did the zone shut off?
text: Yes, it shut off It was running from the controller No, still running Continue

title: Controller off. Voltage check on the zone terminal.
text: Meter to VAC, leads on COM and the zone terminal. Over 18 VAC with the controller off Power cycle, then retest Under 18 VAC Problem is probably at the valve

title: After unplugging, counting to three, and plugging back in — still over 18 VAC?
text: Yes, still reading voltage Continue No, it cleared Controller had latched

title: Remove the valve wire and test at the terminal again.
text: Still reading voltage at the terminal  No reading at the terminal Now read between common and the zone wire

title: What is the zone doing?
text: Troubleshoot one zone at a time. Read the notes below before starting. Valve not coming on A single zone will not start No valves coming on Nothing on the controller runs Valve pulsing on and off Chattering, cycling, or not opening fully Valve not turning on all the way Opens weakly or partially Valve staying on Will not shut off

title: This is usually not an electrical problem. Is the solenoid buzzing?
text: An audible buzz often points to low voltage or a shorted solenoid, but not always. Some solenoids simply buzz. Yes, it is buzzing Often low voltage or a shorted solenoid — work through the electrical side No buzzing Work through the electrical side to confirm

title: Check the display on the controller.
text: Some controllers use indicator lights instead of a message. It shows a fuse fault Check the fuse and replace it if blown, then continue It shows a zone fault Note the zone number No fault shown Display looks normal

title: Is there a wire connected to the terminal for that zone?
text: No wire on the terminal That is your answer There is a diode or zone doubler Beyond what this guide covers Wire is present and landed Continue

title: Resistance check at the controller.
text: Turn the controller OFF. Put the meter on ohms, one lead on COM and one on the zone terminal. Between 20 and 60 Ω Wires and solenoid are probably good — check that the display shows no k or M Below 20 Ω Usually a short Above 60 Ω Usually a bad solenoid

title: Voltage check at the controller.
text: Turn the zone on. Meter to VAC, leads on COM and the zone terminal. No steady reading over 18 VAC Compare against a known working zone Reading present but not 24–30 VAC Power cycle and retest Between 24 and 30 VAC Controller output is good

title: Go to the valve. Remove the splice and check the solenoid by itself.
text: Solenoid reads 20–60 Ω Solenoid is good — problem is in the wiring Solenoid reads out of range Replace it and try the zone

title: Did the zone run with the new solenoid?
text: Yes, it runs now Bad solenoid — done Still will not run Keep going

title: Voltage check at the valve.
text: Turn the zone on. Meter to VAC, leads on the common and the zone wire coming from the controller. Most solenoids need at least 18 VAC. Over 18 VAC at the valve Power is getting there Under 18 VAC at the valve Power is being lost in the wire — split the splice from the run

title: Separate the splice and keep the zone wire and the common apart at the valve. Go back to the controller and read resistance on that zone.
text: With the solenoid out and the two wires apart, nothing connects them but the cable itself, so this should read open (OL). Anything else means the two conductors are touching somewhere in the run. Open (OL) The conductors are not touching — continue Reads a low value or continuity The zone wire and common are shorted together somewhere in the run

title: Now twist the zone wire and the common together at the valve, go back to the controller, and read resistance on that zone again.
text: This takes the solenoid out of the circuit. What is left is the wire run out and back, so the reading tells you whether the conductor is intact. About 5 Ω or less Wire run is intact — the fault was in the splice Still high, or open There is a break between the valve and the controller

title: First, rule out the water side.
text: Try turning on a different valve on the same controller and the same main line. An isolation valve may be closed, or there may be a master valve problem. Other zones run fine Water side is good — continue electrically Nothing runs on that main Check isolation valves and the master valve first
